Thanks very much to everyone who came by today! :D It was really nice to meet all of you, and I'm so glad to see all the interest in metaprogramming. :)

Now that we've kicked off, future cafés will get right into discussions. :) And specifically, they'll be a lot more collaborative! For instance, next time we'll work together on making example tactic. And I do mean together: we'll be passing off the coding from person to person.

A fair number of you are interested in writing tactics for math, and while we peeked under the hood today to get a flavor of the big picture, we didn't see much in the way of how to actually get started doing metaprogramming! So (without sacrificing insight!) hopefully these more hands-on opportunities will help with that. Lean has many "friendly" entry points for metaprogramming, which nicely smooth over many of the internals; you don't need to become an expert to start metaprogramming, and next session we'll see several of these friendlier entry points, like macros, elabs, syntax. :) But we'll still keep an eye on what's "actually" happening when we use them!

In building this tactic we'll likely touch on some of the following: metavariables, unification, Qq, and how Lean expressions work under the hood, term elaboration, do notation, and the tactic state. Of course, we won't get through all of them in a single café; these will be recurring topics, and certainly not the only time we'll engage with them. :)

Also, the need for better metaprogramming learning resources came up multiple times today. Maybe we can grow one together through these gatherings. :) To that end we'll start simple, with a document for free-form collaborative notes which we can all add to during the café: questions, scrapbooking of useful tidbits, insights, gotchas, etc. Eventually this may form the basis for another learning resource.

Re: timing: I'd love to make things work for those in other time zones (or who simply have a conflict)! I am continuing to think about this and considering the options on my end (moving the time some weeks? Adding a second time?). I'll make a poll soon to get a sense of preferred times.

Following yesterday Café @Thomas Murrills suggested that I share the following code as a nice example of level issues.

I'm trying to write some code that match against probability kernel expressions using Qq. However, to actually use the code with Lean Expr, I need to use some inferTypeQ' which can lead to some issue regarding the universe levels involved in the Kernel type:

import Mathlib

open ProbabilityTheory Qq Lean MeasureTheory Meta

def fooQ {u v : Level} {α : Q(Type u)} {β : Q(Type v)} {mα : Q(MeasurableSpace $α)} {mβ : Q(MeasurableSpace $β)}
    (κ : Q(Kernel $α $β)) : MetaM Unit := do
  match κ with
  | ~q($κ ∘ₖ $η) => logInfo m!"Matched composition: {κ} ∘ₖ {η}"
  | ~q($κ) => logInfo m!"Matched kernel: {κ}"
  | _ => logInfo m!"No match for: {κ}"

def foo (κ : Expr) : MetaM Unit := do
  let ⟨.max _u _v, ~q(@Kernel.{_u, _v} $α $β $mα $mβ), κ⟩ ← inferTypeQ' κ | throwError "Expected {κ} : {← inferType κ} to be a Kernel"
  fooQ q($κ)

Explicitly naming _u and _v allows this code to typecheck, but this throws an error:

run_meta foo q(Kernel.const ℝ (ℙ : Measure ℝ))

I believe the reason is that the universe level of Kernel ℝ ℝ is actually directly inferred as 0 instead of max 0 0, which makes the matching to fail. To make it work, one can replace the inferTypeQ' line by

let ⟨.zero, ~q(@Kernel $α $β $mα $mβ), κ⟩ ← inferTypeQ' κ | throwError "Expected {κ} : {← inferType κ} to be a Kernel"

I guess one fix in this specific example would be to perform a regular match against the universe level of κ to decide which "Qq matching" to use.

  return ⟨← instantiateLevelMVars u, ⟨⟩⟩

  return ⟨← instantiateMVarsQ e, ⟨⟩⟩


def foo (κ : Expr) : MetaM Unit := do
  let ⟨u, α, κ⟩ ← inferTypeQ κ
  let .some ⟨u, v, α, b, mα, mβ, hu, h⟩ :

        (hu : u =QL max u' v' + 1) ×' $α =Q @Kernel.{u', v'} $α' $β' $mα $mβ)
    ← (withNewMCtxDepth do
      let u' ← mkFreshLevelMVar
      let v' ← mkFreshLevelMVar
      let α' ← mkFreshExprMVarQ q(Type u')
      let β' ← mkFreshExprMVarQ q(Type v')
      let mα ← mkFreshExprMVarQ q(MeasurableSpace $α')
      let mβ ← mkFreshExprMVarQ q(MeasurableSpace $β')
      let .defEq _ ← isLevelDefEqQ ql(u) ql(max u' v' + 1) | pure none
      let .defEq _ ← isDefEqQ q($α) q(@Kernel.{u', v'} $α' $β' $mα $mβ) | pure none
      let ⟨u', _⟩ ← instantiateLevelMVarsQ u'
      let ⟨v', _⟩ ← instantiateLevelMVarsQ v'
      let ⟨α', _⟩ ← instantiateMVarsQ' q($α')
      let ⟨β', _⟩ ← instantiateMVarsQ' q($β')
      let ⟨mα, _⟩ ← instantiateMVarsQ' q($mα)
      let ⟨mβ, _⟩ ← instantiateMVarsQ' q($mβ)
      return some ⟨u', v', α', β', mα, mβ, ⟨⟩, ⟨⟩⟩) | throwError "Term didn't match"

  let ⟨0, ~q(Prop), e⟩ ← inferTypeQ' e | throwError "not a prop"

I have an issue that I would like to explore in the Café:

Here in the introduction of Metaprogramming in Lean 4, the following example is given:

macro:max x:ident ":" t:term " ↦ " y:term : term
=>
  `(fun $x : $t => $y)

But that breaks parsing of type ascription:

#eval (x : X) -- unexpected token ...

Here is the question on https://live.lean-lang.org with two followup questions.
I feel like this exhibits a very essential gotcha of the extensible parsing framework to know about. As far as I remember, it is not even mentioned in Metaprogramming in Lean 4 (yet).

Sebastian Miele said:

In the first Café, you used macros #show_stx and #show_stx!. I did not find them in Lean or Mathlib + dependencies.

Ah yes, those are Meta Café specials :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes: Mine are still quite simple:

elab tk:"#show_stx" ppLine colGe cmd:command : command => do
  logInfoAt tk m!"{format cmd}"; elabCommand cmd
elab tk:"#show_stx!" ppLine colGe cmd:command : command => do

(There's no real need for the pretty-printing directive ppLine, since nothing is going to pretty-print these, but I was in a pretty-printing mood when I wrote them... :upside_down:)

Some tweaks to note:

  • I use format and repr here; the default instance of ToMessageData you'd get with m!"{stx}" basically just reprints the syntax we already see in source.
  • This only logs it at the #show_stx(!) tokens. This means you don't see it in the infoview when your text cursor is within cmd, which is good if it's very bulky.
  • colGe just demands that #show_stx is not indented more than cmd, to prevent certain confusions.
  • We also elaborate the command and so get to interact with it (hovers, messages, infoview) normally.

Thanks everyone for coming earlier today! :D Thanks to @Sebastian Miele for proposing a neat topic that sent us down a rabbit hole, and to @Robin Arnez for sharing some very useful parser expertise in a confusing situation (as well as for sharing general expertise throughout!) :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

To recap:

We started off by investigating the macro above, and noted that it could be resolved with syntax atomic(ident ":" term " ↦ ") y:term : term to backtrack appropriately. @Snir Broshi noted that it could also be resolved with syntax ident atomic(":" term " ↦ ") y:term : term, and this was confusing... Robin figured out why we had seen the specific failure we saw in the first place, and why both worked. I've written down Robin's explanation in the notes—or, at least, my understanding of it. So any errors are mine :)

  • We then dove further into the underlying infrastructure behind syntax commands, parsing, and antiquotations, and touched on hygiene.
  • Then, we moved onto an intro to fvarIds, bvars, and mvars. We touched on:
    • how the meaning for FVarIds was stored in the LocalContext as LocalDecls
    • how the meaning for MVarIds was stored in the MetavarContext, and each metavariable has its own LocalContext stored in {the MetavarDecl associated to the MVarId in the MetavarContext's ledger}
    • how there's also an ambient LocalContext, and you've got to manage this one with e.g. withMainContext in TacticM or g.withContext (g : MVarId) more generally
    • how bound variable .bvar n's are de Bruijn indices, and
    • how forallTelescope/lambdaTelescope (and friends) let you convert bound variables to free variables, and how mkForallFVars/mkLambdaFVars let you go in reverse and convert free variables to bound variables.

I've made a bunch of more detailed notes on this session in the shared notes document. (I forgot to mention this document entirely at the start of this session—sorry about that!)

As always please feel free to continue the conversation here! :)

I'd also like to point out two things I realized I may have forgotten to mention:

  • The Expr.letE constructor also has a body (corresponding to the part following the semicolon in surface syntax), and can bind variables (.bvars, as usual) in this body.
  • If you know all the data necessary to make a free variable, you can just append one to the local context with withLocalDecl or withLocalDeclD (the same, but .default BinderInfo). As with other with* functions, these modify the context (only) within the following continuation/do block. So make sure the free variable you've created doesn't appear in whatever data you might return from this do block, as it'll be an unknown free variable in the outer context!

After the discussions from last time, I decided to make a PR (lean4#13792) with a parser tracing framework. To use it, you just need to set your lean-toolchain to leanprover/lean4-pr-releases:pr-release-13792 and can then use the command #trace_parse_command. Here's an example from the problem we discussed last time:

syntax ident " : " term " ↦ " term : term

#trace_parse_command "#check (n : Nat)"


You can see that «term_:_↦_» failed with a score of (15, (0, 1000)) but the identifier parser succeeded with a worse score of (10, (1, 1000)) (score means (position, success, priority), ordered lexicographically), so it prioritized the failure. So all candidate parsers end up failing but e.g. (_ : _) × _ ends up having a higher score of (16, (0, 1000)), so that's the error being shown.

#check_failure WP e @ E {{ Φ }}
#check_failure WP e @ E ? {{ Φ }}

But there may surface another problem. withForbidden works on an Option Token value in the parser state, not on a set/list of tokens. withForbidden seems to be used only in some select places in Lean for now, see the references of withForbidden. With two nested uses of withForbidden, the inner one just overwrites the outer one. But because of the structure of your syntax (there always follows a wpPostcond after a wpExpr can become a term) this may not be a problem at all. In fact, it may even be correct, to place the whole wp syntax in a withoutForbidden, because it effectively acts like a bracketing construct. (WP as left bracket, wpPostcond as right brachet.)

There is a register_parser_alias withoutForbidden in Lean.Parser, but no such thing for withForbidden, so I assume that only the former works with syntax.

The following is just a note for anyone who might find it interesting, too. I found the use of ParserResolution in elabTraceParse very instructive. It gives a complete classification of all possible ways a parser currently can be defined in Lean:

import Lean
open Lean Elab Command Parser

instance (α : Type) : Repr (AliasValue α) where
  reprPrec x _ := match x with
  | .const _ => "const" | .unary _ => "unary" | .binary _ => "binary"

deriving instance Repr for ParserResolution

elab tk:"resolve_parser " id:ident : command => do
  let res ← liftCoreM <| resolveParserName id
  logInfoAt tk (repr res)

-- Category parsers
declare_syntax_cat c
resolve_parser term -- [Lean.Parser.ParserResolution.category `term]
resolve_parser c    -- [Lean.Parser.ParserResolution.category `c]

-- `ParserDescr` parser and `Parser` parser
syntax a := "a"
def b : Parser := "b"
resolve_parser a -- [Lean.Parser.ParserResolution.parser `a true]
resolve_parser b -- [Lean.Parser.ParserResolution.parser `b false]

-- Parser aliases defined in `Lean.Parser`, const, unary, binary
resolve_parser ws     -- [Lean.Parser.ParserResolution.alias const]
resolve_parser many1  -- [Lean.Parser.ParserResolution.alias unary]
resolve_parser orelse -- [Lean.Parser.ParserResolution.alias binary]

I'll elaborate a bit more on how I now understand the issue thanks to Robin Arnez and Henrik Böving: When rw looks for the LHS in the goal it uses docs#Lean.Meta.isDefEq to compare the LHS to subexpressions (which you can trace with set_option trace.Meta.isDefEq true), and isDefEq first normalizes the two sides to glossary#whnf (which you can trace with set_option trace.Meta.whnf true) before (somehow) comparing them.

Using ! to denote the strange 1, when f has no value then checking f (n + 1) = f (n + !) with isDefEq checks f = f and n + 1 = n + ! which both hold (under reducible transparency).
But when f is Nat.rec ... then the LHS normalizes to f n + 1 while the RHS normalizes to itself, then isDefeq checks f n + 1 = f (n + !), and both sides are applications so it checks HAdd.hAdd = Nat.rec and says no.

So the whnf depends on the instance being used even though the instances are defeq (under instances transparency). Why is that?
docs#Lean.Meta.whnfImp calls whnfCore, which on function applications calls reduceRec which calls cleanupNatOffsetMajor and as its docstring says it tries to reduce Nat.rec.
It calls isOffset?, which in the case of addition calls evalNat, which in the case of OfNat asserts isInstOfNatNat, which checks that the instance being used is specifically docs#instOfNatNat. The docstring explains why this is strange.

So the "bug" is that the whnf algorithm hardcodes the specific instance instead of checking something like isDefEq theGivenInstance instOfNatNat under instances transparency, which would've let whnf to reduce the Nat.rec on both sides, fixing the issue. Whether this fix is worth it depends on the performance hit such a change will cause in mathlib.
But this is not strictly speaking a bug, since defeq checking is known to be undecidable and so the actual algorithm is an approximation which cannot be perfect. E.g. removing whnf's special handling of Nat.rec entirely would also fix this issue, but probably break many other things.

That means that there’s a second turnstile, and a second group of hypotheses, and a different sort of intro that brings things from a new sort of logical connective one side of the new turnstile to the other, (and thus into the embedded local context, but not into the “real” local context)…this all puts Iris Lean tactics in the interesting position of effectively making a second, domain-specific tactic state.

Thanks to everyone who came out to the Meta Café yesterday! :) @Snir Broshi suggested we take a look at this bug in show, wherein show thing_that_doesn't_exist fails, but does so with no error on show, instead closing the goal silently with sorry. Quite reasonably Snir thought this might take 15 minutes or so. This was not the case. :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

It turned out that the culprit was ultimately Lean's handling of choice nodes in tactic syntax (evalChoice). Since we were overriding the show syntax to log a linter message, both our new syntax parser for show and the original one succeeded. When two parsers of the same priority succeed, Lean effectively just keeps both, and puts them in a new "choice node" in the syntax (whose syntax kind is just choice and whose children are the successful parses). Choice nodes have their own special elaborators in each syntax category.

We found there are two issues with evalChoice, the first of which was actually irrelevant:

  1. evalChoice wraps evalTactic in logic that says "if you throw an internal unsupported syntax error, try the next tactic. In all other cases, either succeed or pass along the thrown exception to the top level". However, evalTactic already catches internal unsupported syntax errors and wraps them in a user-friendly error! So it is impossible to hit the "try the next tactic" branch. (This was irrelevant to the issue.)
  2. evalChoice uses TacticM's try/catch when re-throwing the error. TacticM's try/catch resets the state, which includes resetting the messages! Hence if the thrown error is silent for some reason and expects the noisy errors to have been logged earlier as messages (instead of being part of the thrown exception itself), we will not see any error. This is what was happening.

In particular, elabTerm implicitly creates this behavior. When it hits an error (like an unknown identifier), it (by default) logs the error, puts a synthetic sorry in place of the failure, and keeps on going. The rest of the code (in this case, of the original show) then gets run using that synthetic sorry. When that code inevitably fails, it throws an exception which includes in that exception's bundled MessageData an expression that contains a synthetic sorry.

This is important, since when lean eventually logs the MessageData in this thrown exception (see logAt), it checks (1) if it's an error-style message (2) if it has a synthetic sorry somewhere in it. If both are true, it just doesn't log the message. (Note: each MessageData.ofLazy can actually choose what exactly the logic is to say "yes" or "no", but usually it means "some expression involved has a synthetic sorry".)

So at the end of the day

  1. the overlapping syntax produced a choice node
  2. evalChoice (which elaborates it) wrongly resets the state when re-throwing an error, obliterating logged messages (incl. those produced during elaboration of shows term argument)
  3. the re-thrown error contains a synthetic sorry (since it came from an elaboration failure) and so lean doesn't log it (because it expects those previously logged messages to still exist)

Hence, show silently fails. (And in the course of that failure closes the goal with a sorry too, but that's incidental and not explicitly covered in the above story.) See the linked zulip message above for a MWE :)

The solution is to intervene at the beginning, and give the syntax (priority := high) so that it does not produce a choice node, and truly overrides the syntax it's trying to override instead of relying on choice node semantics! (@Chris Henson followed through with this in #42264 after the café—thanks!!)

We then moved onto discussing the no implicit lambda feature, in the course of illustrating differences with the handling of choice nodes during term elaboration (as opposed to tactic elaboration above). Term elaboration tries all possibilities in the choice node and only succeeds if exactly one of them was successful. Turns out this is rather involved too!

Tracing the logic of disabling the feature with @ on syntax with a choice node revealed that elabChoice should probably call implicitLambda := false, as the outer elaboration of the choice node will have already performed the implicit lambda insertion if necessary. If you don't do this, @ in front of a choice node may behave differently than in front of no choice node.

Anyway, thanks again to the attendees and especially to those who contributed their meta expertise here: @Robin Arnez, @Aaron Liu, @Jovan Gerbscheid :) This session dealt with quite a niche and specific area of Lean (choice nodes and the implicit lambda feature)! It's always nice to be able to dive into an area like that :)

Specifically, we ran into the problem that if your Qq expression lives inside a structure on which you have API, destructuring that structure with e.g. let { a, b, c, .. } := s breaks the connection between the projected field values and the structure instance itself.

Well, take this:

structure MyStruct where
  foo : Nat
  bar : Nat

def test (x : MyStruct) : IO Unit := do
  let { foo, bar } := x
  have : x.foo = foo := rfl -- fails

def test (x : MyStruct) : IO Unit := do
  let foo := x.foo
  let bar := x.bar
  have : x.foo = foo := rfl -- works

Last week in the Meta Café, we discussed how visibility works in the module system! We saw how public imports chain together (and private ones don't), how the different pieces of data of a declaration (name & type, rewriting rule & body) can have separate visibilities (@[expose] for the latter), and how Lean converts declarations to axioms behind the scenes when importing downstream (always for theorems, and whenever @[expose] is absent for definitions).

We also went on a (useful) tangent about the transparency hierarchy and how it governs unfolding (and the difference between transparency settings on declarations and the ambient transparency mode—neither of which are to be confused with transparency hints stored in a declaration, which influence what gets unfolded first as opposed to under what circumstances), and how @[expose] is the precondition for unfolding at all. We also touched on rfl and the auto-applied @[defeq] attribute which complains if your proof is syntactically rfl and you don't have appropriate exposure.

At the end, we investigated why tactic analysis linters in the nightly regression set were failing with "Unknown declaration". The eventual culprit: a call to getConstInfo to find all transitively used constants, which breaks due to set_option backward.privateInPublic true allowing private declarations to seep into the public scope upstream. When downstream imports the public declarations using them, the private ones are unknown and getConstInfo can't look anything up.
